paragraphs: This paper studies how teammates should coordinate against an opponent when they can plan together beforehand but cannot communicate during play. The setting is a zero-sum game with imperfect information. The team chooses a shared probability distribution over strategy profiles, each specifying a strategy for every teammate, and samples a profile before the game begins.

The authors connect the problem of finding that distribution to research on correlation in extensive-form games. They also introduce an algorithm that limits how many strategy profiles a solution may use. Raising this limit produces an anytime approach that can progressively expand the available plan. They find that a small number of carefully selected profiles often suffices for optimal team utility, making coordination easier to describe.

Building on these ideas, the paper develops a column-generation algorithm for finding an optimal distribution. On benchmark games solvable by the previous leading method, it reports a thousandfold speedup. It also solves several previously unsolved games, extending the practical reach of optimal team coordination.
icml-2021-connecting-optimal-ex-ante-col.tldr: A connection to extensive-form correlation yields faster algorithms for optimal team coordination before play, often using only a few strategy profiles.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning lets multiple agents train collaboratively without a central parameter server. Strong performance can depend on the agents receiving statistically similar data, an assumption that often fails in practice. This paper addresses the resulting problem: local learning updates must account for differences between agents’ datasets if collaboration is to remain effective.

Cross-Gradient Aggregation gives each agent information about how its own model behaves on neighboring agents’ data. These cross-gradients describe changes to that model’s parameters evaluated against the neighbors’ datasets. The agent aggregates this information and uses a quadratic programming problem to construct a projected gradient for its update. Inspired by continual learning, the approach makes neighboring data directly relevant to the local update direction.

The authors analyze convergence and evaluate the method on non-IID versions of MNIST and CIFAR-10. Their comparisons report better learning performance than existing leading decentralized algorithms. The improvement also persists when exchanged information is compressed, indicating that the tested benefits can coexist with reduced communication between peers.
icml-2021-cross-gradient-aggregation-for.tldr: Cross-Gradient Aggregation uses neighboring datasets to guide local updates and improves decentralized learning on tested non-IID data, including with compressed communication.

paragraphs: Neural networks can reconstruct images from corrupted measurements, but strong results often require large, varied training collections. For MRI, obtaining those collections can be difficult or expensive. This paper asks whether data augmentation can reduce the amount of training data needed for accelerated MRI reconstruction while preserving reconstruction performance.

The proposed pipeline, MRAugment, is built around invariances in medical imaging measurements. This design matters because a reconstruction example links an image to the physical process that produced its measurements. The authors report that naive augmentation strategies fail when they ignore that physics. MRAugment therefore adapts augmentation to the measurement problem rather than simply transferring classification-oriented strategies.

Across multiple datasets, augmentation prevents overfitting in the low-data setting and can match or exceed leading performance with substantially less training data. Its gains diminish when plentiful data is already available. The experiments also show improved robustness to several shifts in the test distribution, suggesting that the pipeline helps both data efficiency and performance under the tested changes.
icml-2021-data-augmentation-for-deep-lea.tldr: MRAugment uses measurement-aware augmentation to improve MRI reconstruction with limited training data and increase robustness to tested distribution shifts.

paragraphs: This paper compresses high-dimensional data while preserving the information needed to approximate an aggregate geometric objective: the sum of distances from data points to a target shape. Here, a shape can be any set of points, provided it lies within a k-dimensional subspace. The guarantee covers a family of possible shapes rather than one predetermined target.

The procedure constructs a subspace whose dimension is O(k³/ε⁶). For each input point, it keeps both the projection onto that subspace and the distance to it. Together, these quantities suffice for the stated ε-approximation. Keeping the distance alongside the projection is part of the guarantee; the compressed representation contains more than the projected coordinates alone.

The result applies to k-median, subspace approximation, and specified subspace-clustering problems. Storage scales with (n+d)k³/ε⁶ rather than the original number of nonzero matrix entries, which can reach nd. The paper provides running-time guarantees, including a faster dense-matrix variant, and uses the reduction to construct small coresets for two of the covered objectives.
icml-2021-dimensionality-reduction-for-t.tldr: A projection plus each point’s distance to the projection subspace preserves approximate sums of distances to any shape contained in a k-dimensional subspace.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems take a graph as input and have several distinct plausible outcomes. A single predicted value cannot express that structure of uncertainty. This paper introduces Graph Mixture Density Networks, which estimate an output distribution conditioned on a graph and can represent multiple modes, or separate concentrations of likely outcomes.

The models combine graph representation learning with mixture models. Graph representation learning supplies information about the input’s connections, while the mixture component supplies a flexible description of possible outputs. The framework accepts graphs of arbitrary topology, allowing it to address conditional density estimation problems where connectivity and the form of uncertainty both matter.

The authors evaluate the approach on a new benchmark using random graphs and stochastic epidemic simulations. Accounting for both graph structure and multiple outcome modes significantly improves the likelihood assigned to epidemic outcomes. Two real-world regression tasks further demonstrate its ability to model predictive uncertainty. These findings support treating uncertainty as a distribution shaped by the input graph, rather than reducing the task to a single outcome estimate.
icml-2021-graph-mixture-density-networks.tldr: Graph Mixture Density Networks combine graph representations with mixture models to predict multimodal outcome distributions and model uncertainty.

paragraphs: Learning from several source domains becomes harder when their data and computations must stay decentralized. Conventional unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation assumes direct access to source data. Without that access, methods cannot straightforwardly compare source and target examples, and communication costs constrain how the different participants can cooperate.

KD3A addresses this setting through knowledge distillation from models trained on different source domains. Source models become the means of transferring knowledge for adaptation while respecting the decentralized data constraint. The paper also addresses negative transfer: irrelevant or malicious sources can hurt the target model, especially when users cannot control the quality of the contributing datasets.

The experiments report that KD3A substantially outperforms leading unsupervised multi-source adaptation approaches. They also show robustness to negative transfer and a hundredfold reduction in communication cost relative to other decentralized methods in this setting. These results matter together: useful adaptation must manage source quality as well as the practical cost of obtaining knowledge from distributed participants.
icml-2021-kd3a-unsupervised-multi-source.tldr: KD3A adapts through knowledge distillation from decentralized source models, with reported gains in accuracy, negative-transfer robustness, and communication efficiency.

paragraphs: Ordinary supervised classification assumes that every test example belongs to a class represented during training. Open-set learning allows test examples from previously unseen classes. This changes what successful generalization requires: the learner’s behavior on unknown classes becomes part of the problem, beyond distinguishing the classes it has already encountered.

The paper develops a theoretical account of this setting using ideas from transfer learning and probably approximately correct learning theory. Its analysis explicitly investigates the target classifier’s risk on unknown classes. For a training sample of size n, the authors obtain an estimation-error result approaching an order of 1/√n in probability. This concerns the estimation error, rather than asserting that all classification error disappears at that rate.

The theory motivates an algorithm called auxiliary open-set risk, or AOSR. Experiments support its effectiveness. The contribution thus links a generalization analysis to a concrete learning method: it provides a way to reason about performance across training samples while explicitly including the unknown-class behavior that distinguishes open-set learning.
icml-2021-learning-bounds-for-open-set-l.tldr: The paper derives an open-set generalization bound by analyzing unknown-class risk and uses that theory to develop the AOSR algorithm.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy allows clients to randomize reports before sending them to a server for statistical analysis or learning. A practical obstacle is message size: strong algorithms can require large transmissions, particularly for histograms with many possible values or models with many dimensions. This paper studies how to reduce that communication burden.

The authors give a general compression approach for every efficient locally private algorithm under standard cryptographic assumptions. The result preserves privacy and utility guarantees up to negligible losses. In typical applications, a report can be reduced to the size of the server’s pseudorandom-generator seed. The cryptographic assumptions are part of this guarantee, and the stated preservation permits negligible changes.

The paper then derives low-communication methods for frequency estimation and high-dimensional mean estimation. It reports that these methods are simpler and more accurate than existing low-communication alternatives for those tasks. The broader significance is a general route from efficient private reporting to compact reporting, with concrete statistical applications illustrating the resulting benefits.
icml-2021-lossless-compression-of-effici.tldr: Under standard cryptographic assumptions, efficient locally private reports can be compressed with negligible losses in privacy and utility.

paragraphs: This paper studies posterior sampling for model-based reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces. The central issue is balancing actions that gather useful information with actions that earn reward. Posterior sampling represents uncertainty over environment models and uses sampled models to guide learning and control.

Assuming rewards and transitions can be modeled through Bayesian linear regression, the authors prove a regret bound of Õ(H³ᐟ²d√T), where H is episode length, d is state-action dimension, and T is total interaction time. This matches the cited best-known bound for non-posterior-sampling methods in linear MDPs. A feature-based extension handles nonlinear representations, replacing d with the representation dimension when linear kernels are used on those features.

The practical algorithm, MPC-PSRL, combines posterior sampling with model predictive control for action selection. Bayesian linear regression on a neural network’s penultimate layer captures model uncertainty. On benchmark continuous-control tasks, the authors report leading sample efficiency compared with prior model-based methods and eventual performance matching model-free methods, connecting the theoretical study to a practical control approach.
icml-2021-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: The paper establishes conditional regret guarantees for continuous-space posterior sampling and introduces a sample-efficient control algorithm combining it with model predictive control.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify individual anomalous entries in a low-rank matrix when ordinary entries also contain substantial noise. Motivated by retail and inventory management, it addresses a mismatch with approaches that require noise in non-anomalous entries to become vanishingly small. The model instead allows sub-exponential noise.

The proposed method detects anomalies entry by entry and accommodates a general family of probabilistic anomaly models. Its theoretical foundation extends matrix-completion guarantees from recovering overall structure to controlling errors at individual entries. The analysis allows missing observations and corruption of a fraction of entries by an unknown anomaly model, combining incomplete data with uncertainty about how anomalies arise.

Treating detection as classification, the authors obtain a minimax-optimal detection rate up to logarithmic factors. This qualifies the optimality claim while showing that the rate approaches the best worst-case performance for the studied setting. Evaluation on data from a large consumer-goods retailer reports substantial improvements over incumbent detection methods, supplying practical evidence alongside the statistical guarantee.
icml-2021-near-optimal-entrywise-anomaly.tldr: An entrywise anomaly detector handles noisy, incomplete low-rank matrices and achieves a minimax-optimal detection rate up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Latent variable models explain observed data through quantities that are not directly observed. Estimating their parameters can become difficult when hidden structure is complex, variables mix continuous and discrete forms, parameters are constrained, or datasets are large. This paper targets estimation methods that can address such general latent-variable problems.

The authors propose a gradient-based method that uses variance reduction to accelerate estimation. The central methodological choice is to improve the gradient-based estimation procedure through that variance-reduction mechanism. This matters because a useful estimator must offer manageable computation as well as desirable statistical behavior; improving one without retaining the other would leave an important part of the problem unresolved.

The paper proves convergence under model assumptions described as general and mild. It also establishes better computational complexity than classical gradient methods while retaining favorable statistical properties. Numerical results support the theoretical analysis. Together, these findings present variance reduction as a way to make estimation more computationally efficient within the analyzed class of latent variable models.
icml-2021-on-estimation-in-latent-variab.tldr: A variance-reduced gradient method accelerates latent-variable estimation with convergence guarantees and improved computational complexity under the paper’s assumptions.

paragraphs: Biclustering groups both the rows and the columns of a data matrix, revealing structure that depends on the two groupings together. This paper studies parameter estimation for statistical models with such hidden structure. The latent variables make direct maximum-likelihood estimation prohibitively difficult in practice, motivating the use of variational inference as a more tractable approach.

The authors establish a precise estimation-error bound for the variational estimator. Under mild assumptions in the biclustering setting, the bound matches the minimax rate: its error scales at the best achievable worst-case rate for the modeled problem. This gives theoretical support to an approximation method whose practical usefulness has outpaced the available guarantees.

The paper also analyzes coordinate ascent variational inference, providing both local and global convergence results. These address algorithmic behavior, complementing the statistical result about estimator accuracy. Numerical experiments validate the theories. The combined contribution concerns both whether the variational estimator can be statistically accurate and how the procedure used to compute it converges.
icml-2021-on-variational-inference-in-bi.tldr: For biclustering models under mild assumptions, variational estimation attains the minimax error rate, with additional convergence results for coordinate ascent.

paragraphs: Value iteration repeatedly updates estimates of how valuable states are in a Markov decision process. Its convergence can be slow when the discount factor is close to one, so distant rewards remain influential. This paper explores whether ideas from control theory can accelerate that iterative calculation.

The key move is to view the sequence of value estimates as a dynamical system. Once the updates are understood this way, controllers can modify how the estimates evolve. The authors develop proportional-derivative, proportional-integral, and proportional-integral-derivative variants of value iteration and analyze their error dynamics. This provides a framework for studying how controller choices affect progress toward the solution.

The paper proves improved convergence rates for certain classes of MDPs and demonstrates improvements empirically for broader classes. These are qualified acceleration results, rather than a claim that every controller speeds up every problem. The authors also propose automatically adapting controller gains and show experimentally that this mechanism is effective, addressing the practical task of selecting the controller’s numerical settings.
icml-2021-pid-accelerated-value-iteratio.tldr: Control-inspired modifications can accelerate value iteration, with proofs for certain MDP classes and broader empirical support.

paragraphs: Training a binary classifier usually requires labels for individual examples. Pairwise supervision offers an alternative, but asking whether two examples share a label can still be difficult when either example’s class is uncertain. This paper introduces a weaker form of supervision: knowing which member of an unlabeled pair is more likely to be positive.

The proposed pairwise comparison setting uses that relative confidence to learn predictions for individual data points. The authors specify a data-generation process and derive an unbiased risk estimator with a theoretical guarantee. This estimator connects the available pair comparisons to the classification objective. They then use correction functions to improve the initial estimator.

A second part of the approach links pairwise comparison classification to learning with noisy labels. That connection produces a progressive risk estimator, further improved through consistency regularization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the methods. The findings suggest that relative positive-class confidence can provide practically useful supervision when direct labels or reliable same-class judgments are difficult to obtain.
icml-2021-pointwise-binary-classificatio.tldr: Pairwise confidence comparisons can train an individual-example binary classifier through theoretically grounded risk estimators and consistency regularization.

paragraphs: A Dirichlet Belief Network learns interpretable hidden distributions through multiple layers. Its depth can be underused when those layers repeatedly develop similar distribution patterns. This paper addresses that representational problem by allowing larger changes between layers, so additional depth can support more flexible hidden structure.

The proposed Poisson-randomised Dirichlet Belief Network inserts Poisson random variables into the connections between layers. A component-wise propagation mechanism allows individual parts of the latent distributions to vary substantially across depth. The authors develop a layer-wise Gibbs sampling algorithm for inference and report a greater number of effective layers than in the original DirBN. They also integrate out latent distributions to obtain an alternative description as a deep integer-valued stochastic network.

The method is evaluated on relational modeling, where the authors report improved link prediction and more interpretable visualizations of latent distributions. These findings connect the architectural change to both predictive performance and interpretability. The contribution centers on making depth more useful by enabling layers to learn meaningfully different distributions.
icml-2021-poisson-randomised-dirbn-large.tldr: Pois-DirBN introduces Poisson variables between layers to increase latent-distribution variation, with reported improvements in link prediction and interpretability.

paragraphs: Policy optimization works well empirically with expressive neural policies, but its exploration behavior is less well understood when function approximation is nonlinear. This paper develops ENIAC, an actor-critic method that permits nonlinear approximation in the critic. The aim is to connect strategic exploration with a theoretical account of uncertainty in that richer function class.

Under assumptions including a bounded eluder dimension d for the critic class, the authors show that the learner finds a near-optimal policy within a number of exploration rounds polynomial in d, up to logarithmic factors. The method also tolerates model misspecification and extends existing linear-approximation results. The exploration guarantee therefore depends on structural assumptions about the function class.

The paper additionally develops computational optimizations with somewhat weaker statistical guarantees and a practical adaptation using existing deep reinforcement-learning tools. Experiments show that this adaptation outperforms prior heuristics inspired by linear methods. The result supports the value of accounting for nonlinear uncertainty explicitly, while the separate optimized variants expose a trade-off between computation and statistical guarantees.
icml-2021-provably-correct-optimization-.tldr: ENIAC gives conditional exploration guarantees with nonlinear critics, and a practical adaptation outperforms tested heuristics derived from linear methods.

paragraphs: Publishers choosing reserve prices for first-price advertising auctions must account for how bidders respond to those prices. This paper proposes an adaptive, gradient-based method for improving reserves. It estimates bidder responsiveness by introducing experimental changes to reserve prices and using the resulting information to guide subsequent updates.

The central contribution is a way to make those gradient estimates less variable. The authors decompose the revenue objective into a demand component and a bidding component, then develop variance-reduction techniques for each. Using the structure of revenue gives the optimization procedure a more targeted treatment of noisy measurements than treating the entire objective as an undifferentiated quantity.

The paper analyzes the bias-variance trade-offs introduced by its techniques and reports improved convergence in both theory and practice. Experiments use synthetic data and real advertising-auction data from a major exchange. These findings support the proposed decomposition as a practical aid to adaptive reserve optimization, with the statistical trade-offs considered explicitly rather than assuming that reducing variance is cost-free.
icml-2021-reserve-price-optimization-for.tldr: Decomposing auction revenue into demand and bidding components enables lower-variance gradient estimates for adaptive first-price reserve optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning with an entropic risk measure, so the learning objective accounts for risk in rewards. It focuses on function approximation, which represents the quantities needed for learning through a chosen function class. The challenge is to combine that approximation with risk-sensitive decision-making while controlling learning performance.

The authors first develop an algorithm using linear function approximation. Existing approaches suffer from inappropriate regularization and biases in regression, so the new method introduces debiasing transformations in both backward induction and regression. They then extend the approach to general function approximation, where the corresponding debiasing transformations are implicit. Both developments address bias within the learning procedure itself.

The paper proves sublinear regret for both algorithms, meaning accumulated regret grows more slowly than the interaction horizon covered by the bounds. It also establishes a trade-off between generality and efficiency. The unified analysis supplies the first reported sublinear regret guarantees for this setting, linking the debiasing approach to a formal account of learning with risk-sensitive objectives.
icml-2021-risk-sensitive-reinforcement-l.tldr: Debiasing transformations yield sublinear-regret algorithms for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning with linear and general function approximation.

paragraphs: A policy that acts from images can become distracted by visual details unrelated to the task. SECANT targets zero-shot generalization: using a learned policy in unseen visual environments with large distribution shifts, without further adaptation there. Its approach separates learning successful behavior from learning a representation that withstands visual variation.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, reinforcement learning trains an expert policy from scratch with weak image augmentations. Next, a student network learns to imitate that expert through supervised learning with strong augmentations. The student’s behavior is anchored by the expert while its representation is trained under stronger visual changes. The authors report that this makes the student more visually robust than its teacher.

Experiments cover control, robotic manipulation, vision-based driving, and indoor object navigation. Average reward improves over previous leading methods by 26.5%, 337.8%, 47.7%, and 15.8%, respectively. These results support separating policy optimization from robust representation learning in the evaluated settings, rather than requiring both objectives to be learned through the same reinforcement-learning stage.
icml-2021-secant-self-expert-cloning-for.tldr: SECANT trains an expert with weak visual augmentation, then a strongly augmented imitation student, improving zero-shot generalization across four tested domains.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization models data organized across several dimensions, but conventional multilinear decompositions can miss complicated interactions. More expressive deep models introduce another challenge when observations arrive continuously: the model needs an efficient way to update its beliefs as new entries appear. This paper develops Streaming Bayesian Deep Tensor factorization, or SBTD, to address both issues.

SBTD uses Bayesian neural networks to model the interactions. Each network weight receives a spike-and-slab prior, encouraging sparse weights and helping prevent overfitting. For inference, the authors combine a multivariate Delta-method approximation with moment matching to approximate the network output’s posterior and compute running model evidence. These calculations support a streaming procedure within assumed-density filtering and expectation propagation.

When new tensor entries arrive, the algorithm incrementally updates the posterior over both latent factors and neural-network weights. It also identifies and suppresses redundant weights as learning proceeds. Results on four real-world applications demonstrate advantages of the approach, supporting the combination of flexible interaction modeling, uncertainty-aware inference, and responsive updates for streaming observations.
icml-2021-streaming-bayesian-deep-tensor.tldr: SBTD combines Bayesian neural tensor factorization with streaming posterior updates and sparse-weight priors to model complex interactions as data arrives.

paragraphs: Minimax models, including generative adversarial networks, involve competing minimization and maximization objectives. Their training algorithm can affect more than convergence speed. This paper studies how that choice also influences generalization, using algorithmic stability to examine how learning behavior changes when the training data changes.

For convex-concave problems, the authors compare gradient descent ascent with the proximal point method. Gradient descent ascent is not guaranteed to achieve vanishing excess risk, while the proximal point method has a bounded excess-risk guarantee in the same setting. The distinction concerns the strength of the available guarantees; a bounded result should not automatically be read as a claim that excess risk vanishes.

For nonconvex-nonconcave problems, the comparison is between stochastic gradient descent ascent and GDmax, which fully solves the maximization problem at every iteration. The analysis suggests an advantage for gradient descent ascent when both sides update simultaneously with similar learning rates. Numerical results illustrate the role of optimization choices in generalization, supporting the paper’s emphasis on the training procedure as part of statistical performance.
icml-2021-train-simultaneously-generaliz.tldr: Stability analysis links minimax optimization choices to generalization and suggests benefits from simultaneous gradient updates with similar learning rates.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a way to compare probability distributions without specifying a fixed parametric form. Its computational cost can make direct use on large datasets difficult, so practitioners often compute comparisons on small subsets, or minibatches. This paper examines what is lost when that convenient approximation replaces a full-data calculation.

The authors argue that minibatch optimal transport can introduce undesirable smoothing. They propose combining minibatches with unbalanced optimal transport as an alternative that can behave more robustly. The contribution therefore retains the computational appeal of subset-based calculations while changing the transport formulation used within them. It addresses a consequence of minibatching itself, rather than treating smaller calculations as automatically faithful substitutes.

The theoretical study covers unbiased estimators, the existence of gradients, and concentration bounds. These properties help characterize estimation and optimization for the proposed approach. In challenging domain-adaptation experiments, unbalanced transport gives substantially better results and competes with or surpasses recent baselines. The evidence supports its usefulness for the tested adaptation problems alongside the analysis of its statistical properties.
icml-2021-unbalanced-minibatch-optimal-t.tldr: Combining minibatches with unbalanced optimal transport addresses undesirable smoothing and improves results on tested domain-adaptation problems.

paragraphs: Encoding a generative adversarial network means mapping real data into latent codes that a generator can turn back into reconstructions. Although earlier theories promised precise reconstruction, practical algorithms often produce noticeable discrepancies. This paper investigates that gap through three theoretical incompatibility results for the encoding-GAN setting it studies.

The first result says that a perfect encoder and generator cannot both be continuous. The second says that neural networks cannot precisely approximate both underlying mappings simultaneously. These results challenge the expectation that a practical encoder-generator pair can simply inherit ideal reconstruction guarantees. They identify tensions involving the two mappings together, rather than treating the encoder’s accuracy as an isolated issue.

The third result establishes a conflict between stability and accuracy in this setting. The authors connect it to training difficulties and the observed trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and disentanglement. Their contribution is explanatory: the principles may help reconcile idealized theories with empirical behavior and inform later network designs. They do not present the results as a universal prohibition on useful GAN reconstructions.
icml-2021-uncertainty-principles-of-enco.tldr: Three theoretical incompatibilities in encoding GANs help explain why ideal reconstruction, continuity, accurate approximation, and stability cannot all be expected together.

paragraphs: Stochastic neural networks inject noise into hidden layers and can achieve strong resistance to adversarial attacks. Existing designs often choose noise heuristically and may still rely on computationally expensive adversarial training. This paper proposes a stochastic network whose noise distribution is learned using a theoretical robustness objective.

The main distinction is the shape of that noise. Isotropic noise treats directions uniformly, whereas the proposed anisotropic distribution can vary by direction. The network learns this distribution by optimizing a learning-theoretic bound on adversarial robustness. This provides a principled target for noise design, connecting the random perturbations inside the network to an explicit robustness analysis.

The authors report leading performance without adversarial training on the benchmarks they evaluate. They also demonstrate applicability across different architectures and robustness against several white-box and black-box attacks. Training is described as simple and fast relative to existing alternatives. Together, these findings support learned directional noise as a practical robustness mechanism, with theoretical motivation and empirical evidence across multiple tested conditions.
icml-2021-weight-covariance-alignment-fo.tldr: Learning direction-dependent hidden-layer noise from a robustness bound yields strong reported adversarial robustness without adversarial training.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised image-learning methods compare augmented views of the same image with examples from other images. The matching views are positives, while the other examples serve as negatives. Using many negatives can be computationally demanding. This paper proposes a different loss built around whitening the learned features.

The key role of whitening is to spread the representations of samples within a batch. This counters a degenerate solution in which every input receives the same representation, collapsing all samples to one point. Preventing that collapse is essential because agreement between views is uninformative if the network represents every image identically. The proposed objective uses the structure of the feature batch to address this issue.

The approach does not require negatives or asymmetric networks. Without negative examples, it can also draw multiple positive pairs from one image. The contribution is thus an alternative design for self-supervised representation learning: whitening supplies an anti-collapse mechanism while allowing learning to be organized around multiple views of the same instance.
icml-2021-whitening-for-self-supervised-.tldr: A whitening-based self-supervised loss prevents representation collapse without negative examples or asymmetric networks.
